content:
One of the things I like with the ext tactic is that I don't need to know the name of the extensionality theorem for my given object.

I was wondering if it would make sense to generalize the ext tactic so that

  • ⊢ f ≠ g would turn into ⊢ ∃ x, f x ≠ g x
  • (h : f = g) ⊢ would turn into (h : ∀ x, f x = g x) ⊢
  • (h : f ≠ g) ⊢ would turn into (x : α) (h : f x ≠ g x) ⊢

Here, I'm using funext_iff just as an example, but it would ideally work for any ext_iff lemma.
I know these are not, strictly speaking, applying extensionality, and would need to be using the ext_iff but it would solve a recurring problem that I face: I usually find the correct ext_iff lemma for my object and then pass it to simp.

Does this make sense? What do you currently use in these situations?
For the second one, I'd expect it to be written ext at h
I guess the third would be ext x at h?

I have been frustrated in the past that for ext_iff lemmas you're forced to find the right name and rewrite with it rather than being able to use ext; I think this would be a nice extension. If people are concerned about feature creep it could be ext! or something. Actually sounds like a nice exercise for beginner tactic writers :-)

Additionally, I would like to allow ext to be used on other relations:

  • ⊢ s ⊆ t and ext x would turn into (x) ⊢ x ∈ s → x ∈ t
  • ⊢ f ≤ g and ext x would turn into (x) ⊢ f x ≤ g x

I imagined that a tactic doing this would be called gext, analogous to grw and gcongr. But of course if ext itself can do it that would be better.

These two examples can currently be done with intro x, but in a way that that relies on defeq abuse and obscures what is actually happening.
I'll give it a go and call it gext for now. But I also would prefer to have ext work normally on the things it already does but then also on these examples.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

These two examples can currently be done with intro x,

Do you have one in mind that can't be?

I didn't have one in mind, but maybe this could be in scope:

import Mathlib

example (a b : Nat × Nat) : a ≤ b := by
  ext -- fails
  -- I would expect to get:
  -- ⊢ a.1 ≤ b.1
  -- ⊢ a.2 ≤ b.2

Note that we do already have

example (a b c d : Nat) : (a, b) ≤ (c, d) := by
  gcongr
  -- ⊢ a ≤ c
  -- ⊢ b ≤ d
